docs.title: Catch-up summary
docs.text:
The master's thesis is complete. Work now runs on three lines:

  • A paper for the journal Computers, Environment and Urban Systems (CEUS), in drafting. It presents the method from the thesis: for each GPS stay, it gives a probability that the person was in a building, on a street, or in an open space, instead of picking one place. The model learns from 907 stays with known answers from a field survey in Hiroshima. On data it has not seen, it picks the correct type for 71.8% of stays (grouped CV accuracy 0.718 ± 0.028), and it does better there than Random Forest and XGBoost. Its main weakness is mistaking streets and open spaces for buildings. For streets, this comes from how the street map is cut into many short pieces, not from the GPS data itself; for open space, the cause is still open. Start from Thesis summary. The three changes from the meeting on 20-10-2026 are now in the draft (CEUS paper): one column; a map of four stays (two indoor, two outdoor) that compares the framework with the usual nearest-place rule, which picks the correct type for only 47.9% of stays; and one street stay shown through every step of the method. Latest update: CEUS paper revisions.
  • CSIS DAYS 2026: everything is ready, the poster (approved by sensei on 20-10-2026) and the slides for the talk; the QR code on the poster opens the slides. Only printing the poster is left (CSIS DAYS 2026).
  • The doctoral plan (Doctoral plan). The goal is an assignment that also knows which stays came before (Sequence-aware assignment). The meeting on 20-10-2026 added three new items, now in the inbox: the indoor and outdoor split across the four seasons, a second level of probability that picks which building, street or open space, and real open spaces in the ground truth. A new review of the key literature, a test in another city and a better way to cut streets into pieces are on hold. The toy GPS data idea was dropped. Latest update: Publications and doctoral plan.

The board below shows every work item by status: Inbox (not started, or still to discuss with sensei), On-going and On-hold. A finished item moves to Done (shown on the Plans page), and its results move into the notes.

The thesis code was checked against the text on 19-10-2026, and every number on this site comes from the checked pipeline. The check is settled and its notes are archived.

docs.title: About this research
docs.text:
Hafiyyan Hilmy Fawwaz · Urban Transportation and Planning Lab, Hiroshima University

A GPS staypoint rarely tells you which place a person actually visited: positional error is often larger than the gap between a building, the street in front of it and the open space beside it. This research builds a probabilistic framework that assigns each staypoint to an urban spatial entity (building, street or open space) under explicit positional uncertainty, instead of snapping it to the nearest one.

docs.title: Alpha calibration
docs.text:
Analysis Master 21-07-2026

How the setting α was chosen. α controls how fast the f_distance score falls as a candidate gets farther from the stay.

The method is called profile likelihood, and it uses Model 4a. Take one value of α, fit all the other weights again, and record how well the model fits (LL(b), closer to 0 is better). Repeat for many values of α and keep the best one. Because \(f_\text{distance}(\alpha) = f_\text{distance}(1)^{1/\alpha^2}\), the scores do not need to be computed again for each α.

α LL(b) Accuracy 1.0 -0.6731 0.714 2.0 -0.6494 0.722 2.4 -0.6463 0.721 2.979 -0.6453 0.727 3.0 -0.6453 0.725 4.0 -0.6461 0.724 5.0 -0.6447 0.728 6.0 -0.6437 0.729

The fit rises quickly up to about α = 2 and is almost flat after that. The optimizer finds an inside best point at α* = 2.979. Every α from about 2.4 upward fits nearly as well (within 1.92 total log-likelihood units, the usual 95% limit), so the data rule out small values of α but do not pin down large ones. Above α ≈ 4 the fit rises slowly again and passes the inside best point near α = 4.6 (by 1.4 total log-likelihood units at α = 6, which is not significant). At such large α, f_distance is close to 1 for almost every candidate, so the per-type f_distance columns act like the type constants rejected in Model 5: alternative-specific constants (rejected). So the inside best point is used. Computing the scores again from scratch at this value gives the same result as the shortcut, to within 2e-16.

  • Model 2 has its own best α (2.275). Using that value in Model 4a costs little (1.5 total log-likelihood units, below the 1.92 that would count as significant), and using Model 4a's α in Model 2 costs almost nothing (0.1). So the two models agree on how fast the score should fall.
  • Tune α once on Model 4a, then build the later models with that value. Tuning α again inside Model 5 gives 2.28 and improves the fit by only 0.3 total log-likelihood units (accuracy +0.4 percentage points). Inside Model 6 with its α = 1 terms it gives 2.45 and improves the fit by 3.0 units (accuracy +0.8 points), but that model is not used: its terms were chosen at α = 1, and it is very unstable at any α (condition number above 140,000). So tuning once loses almost nothing for the models that matter.
  • Model 1 has no inside best point. Its fit is best at the smallest α tried (0.2) and hardly changes over the whole range, and no value of α fixes its main problem (Model 1: base).

The main result of this step: The f_distance² artifact. With the full data, before downsampling, the best α moves: Raw-density alpha profile. Part of Calibration.

docs.title: Candidate density bias toward building
docs.text:
Analysis Master 23-07-2026

Why the model often says "building" when the correct answer is street.

A first guess would be that street stays have too few street candidates. The data shows the opposite. Stays that really were on a street have the most candidates of their own type:

True type Same-type candidates, mean median Total candidates, mean Building 5.99 4 20.77 Street 13.13 11 35.44 Open space 4.25 3 13.79

The share_type term gives a lower value to a candidate with many neighbours of the same type. The penalty is strongest for streets (the weight share_street is -5.16 in the Final model, against -1.18 for buildings). The map stores streets as many short pieces next to each other (Spatial entity layers). So a stay on a street is punished for a crowd of street pieces that the map itself created. The probability then moves to the nearest building (Confusion matrix).

This explains the street errors only. Open-space stays have the fewest candidates of their own type, and share_os is small and not significant (+0.25). So the open-space errors toward building need another explanation, which has not been found yet.

The street part comes from the street map, so it can be fixed. The GPS data itself does not set the limit (Contributions). But it weakens the argument that streets are real places of activity: Tension with the street-space argument, Candidate density as boundary-matching difficulty.

Part of Error analysis.

docs.title: Downsampling shrinks the candidate search area
docs.text:
Analysis Master 29-07-2026

With the same search distance (R_buffer = 10 m), the full survey data produced 32,563 candidate rows, and the downsampled data 20,219. That is 1.6 times more candidates for the same 907 stays.

This is expected. Candidate selection draws a circle around every GPS point of a stay. The full data has about 9.7 times more points, and more circles cover more ground, even with the same radius. So downsampling the data also makes the search area smaller, not only the number of points. Keep this in mind if the search distance is tested again (R_buffer: 10 m vs 15 m).

Part of Raw-density refit.

docs.title: Confusion matrix
docs.text:
Analysis Master 23-07-2026

A table of the Final model's answers against the correct answers. Each row is the correct type, each column is the model's answer. Every answer comes from a test where that stay was not used for learning (grouped cross-validation).

actual predicted building street open space recall building 474 24 33 89.3% street 77 91 17 49.2% open space 95 10 86 45.0%

Recall is the share of stays of one type that the model found. For example, 91 of 185 street stays were called street: 49.2%.

  • The model finds building stays about twice as often as the other two types.
  • When it gets a street or open-space stay wrong, it mostly says building (41.6% and 49.7% of those stays). It rarely mixes up street and open space (9.2% and 5.2%).
  • More open-space stays were called building (95) than open space (86).

On the training data the table looks much the same (building 90.4%, street 51.9%, open space 44.5%). So overfitting does not explain this pattern.

Why it happens for streets: Candidate density bias toward building. How it changes from test set to test set: Fold difficulty. Answers RQ2 of Research questions. Part of Error analysis.

docs.title: Directional scope ablation (3a vs 3b)
docs.text:
Analysis Master 21-07-2026

Is f_directional useful only for streets? Two versions were compared. 3a is Model 2: share-type and sigma unchanged, with the direction score for every candidate. 3b sets the direction score to 0 for buildings and open spaces, so only streets keep it:

\[V_k = w_1 f_\text{distribution} + w_2 f_\text{distance} + w_3 f_\text{dir,street} + w_4\,share_\text{bldg} + w_5\,share_\text{street} + w_6\,share_\text{os} + w_7\,\sigma\]

Both versions have 7 parameters, so they can be compared directly.

R=10 m 3a: shared 3b: street only LL(b) -0.7455 -0.7604 Accuracy 0.663 0.653 Building / street / open space 0.838 / 0.438 / 0.393 0.838 / 0.395 / 0.387 CV accuracy (grouped) 0.655 ± 0.029 0.644 ± 0.023 Condition number 114 231
  • Keeping the score only for streets does not help. The fit is worse and the model is less stable (the direction score's VIF is 8.00 instead of 7.23, and the condition number doubles).
  • It mainly lowers street accuracy; building stays the same.
  • In 3b, share_bldg gets stronger (t goes from 2.79 to 3.50). So how the direction score is set up changes what share_bldg picks up.

3a was kept. The same result came back later with the tuned α, in f_directional: shared vs split. Next: Model 4a: alternative-specific parameters. Part of Calibration.

docs.title: f_directional: shared vs split
docs.text:
Analysis Master 21-07-2026

Does f_directional need a separate weight for each place type ("split", the 13-parameter model, \(w_{3,t} f_\text{directional}\))? Or is one weight for all types enough ("shared", 11 parameters, \(w_3 f_\text{directional}\))? Everything else stayed the same.

Shared (11) Split (13) Street only (11) Accuracy 0.729 0.727 0.724 CV accuracy (grouped) 0.718 ± 0.028 0.710 ± 0.030 0.714 ± 0.024 Condition number 1,869 2,036 1,882

Split vs shared: LR = 4.32, df = 2, p = 0.115. This is not significant: the two extra weights do not improve the fit enough. They improve the fit on the training data a little, but lower accuracy on unseen data and raise the condition number. That is overfitting (Overfitting signature).

The shared weight is clearly significant (t = +6.82). In the split version, the building and street weights pass 1.96, and the street weight turns negative (-5.14). "Street only" is a little worse than shared at this size: lower accuracy on unseen data (0.714 against 0.718), the same fit, slightly lower stability, and lower training accuracy. In the 7-parameter models, shared wins on every measure (CV 0.655 against 0.646), the same result as in Directional scope ablation (3a vs 3b).

Decision: shared, 11 parameters → Final model, the final model of the thesis (Section 5.1.8). Part of Calibration.

docs.title: The f_distance² artifact
docs.text:
Analysis Master 21-07-2026

With α = 1, a squared distance term (f_distance²) looked clearly significant (t = 3.79) in the Interaction term screen (α = 1). After Alpha calibration set α to 2.979, the same test, run again from the start, gives only t = -0.10.

So the squared term was not finding a real curve in the data. It was making up for a distance score that fell too fast because α was too small. It also caused much of the instability of Model 6, where it had the highest VIF (44.5).

Screen term t at α = 1 t at α = 2.979 f_distance² 3.79 -0.10 σ² 4.53 4.76 f_distribution × σ 1.14 1.37 f_distance × f_directional 0.55 1.59 f_distribution × share_type 4.72 4.22

Lesson: after changing α, choose the extra terms again from the start. Keeping the old terms and only changing α made the model far less stable (condition number from 13,815 to 378,776; highest VIF from 44 to 211, on f_distance²).

One case of Overfitting signature. Next: Model 6, re-derived at calibrated alpha. Part of Calibration.

Analysis Master 21-07-2026

How closely each pair of the Final model's 11 inputs move together. A correlation near 1 or -1 means two inputs carry almost the same information. Near 0 means they are unrelated.

The strongest pairs are always inputs of the same type: f_distance and share for open space (.93), street (.91) and building (.89). docs.title: Final model
docs.text:
Analysis Master 21-07-2026

The model the thesis ends with (Section 5.1.8). It has 11 parameters, uses α = 2.979 and a search distance (R_buffer) of 10 m.

\[V_t = w_{1,t} f_\text{distribution} + w_{2,t} f_\text{distance} + w_3 f_\text{directional} + w_{4,t}\,share_t + w_5\,\sigma\]

A small \(t\) means the weight is different for each place type (building, street, open space). No \(t\) means one weight shared by all types.

How well it fits. The most important line is CV accuracy: on data it did not learn from, the model picks the correct type for 71.8% of stays.

LL(0) / LL(C) / LL(b) -1.1318 / -0.9507 / -0.6477 ρ² vs LL(0) / LL(C) 0.428 / 0.319 Accuracy (in-sample) 0.729 CV accuracy (grouped, 5-fold) 0.718 ± 0.028 CV building / street / open space 0.893 / 0.491 / 0.450 Condition number 1,869

The weights. w is the learned weight: positive raises the probability, negative lowers it. t shows how clearly the weight differs from zero (about 2 or more is significant). VIF shows overlap with other inputs (above 10 is the usual warning line; see Multicollinearity is structural).

docs.title: Fold difficulty
docs.text:
Analysis Master 23-07-2026

Cross-validation splits the data into 5 test sets (folds). This table shows the Final model's accuracy in each one:

Fold Total Building Street Open space 0 0.753 0.916 0.649 0.395 1 0.706 0.887 0.459 0.432 2 0.736 0.915 0.500 0.474 3 0.714 0.868 0.486 0.513 4 0.680 0.877 0.361 0.436

Building accuracy hardly changes (0.868-0.916). Street accuracy changes almost 2 times (0.361-0.649). Each fold has about the same number of street stays (36-38), so the changes do not come from small numbers. For street, the two hardest folds (4 and 1) are also the two hardest overall, and the two best (0 and 2) are the two best overall. So for street, the difficulty comes from which stays end up in a fold.

Open space does not follow this pattern. It is low in every fold (0.395-0.513), and its weakest fold (0) is the best fold overall. So its weakness is not a fold effect.

Random Forest and XGBoost agree only in part (ML ceiling check, row level): fold 1 is among the two hardest for all three models, and fold 2 is among the two best for all three. The other folds change places between models.

docs.title: Interaction term screen (α = 1)
docs.text:
Analysis Master 21-07-2026

Could combined or squared terms help the model? Five such terms were tested together, on top of the 7-parameter model with shared weights. An interaction term multiplies two inputs, for example f_distribution × σ. A term with a t-value above about 2 counts as significant.

Term w t f_distance² +4.573 3.79 significant σ² +0.440 4.53 significant f_distribution × σ +0.414 1.14 f_distance × f_directional +0.722 0.55 f_distribution × share_type +4.915 4.72 significant

The three significant terms were added to Model 4a: alternative-specific parameters. This gives Model 6, with 16 parameters:

\[V_t = w_{1,t} f_\text{distribution} + w_{2,t} f_\text{distance} + w_{3,t} f_\text{directional} + w_{4,t}\,share_t + w_5\,\sigma + w_6\,f_\text{distance}^2 + w_7\,\sigma^2 + w_8\,(f_\text{distribution}\times share_\text{type})\] 4a Model 6 (α = 1) Accuracy 0.714 0.716 Building / street / open space 0.872 / 0.514 / 0.471 0.868 / 0.508 / 0.492 CV accuracy (grouped) 0.697 ± 0.026 0.709 ± 0.037 Condition number 739 13,815

Model 6 raises open space further (to 0.492) and lowers building and street a little. Inside the larger model, σ² is no longer significant (t falls to 1.78). And f_distance² turns out to make up for an α that was not yet tuned: The f_distance² artifact.

The two terms that were not significant are built from inputs that overlap strongly (VIF up to 72). So "not significant" is weak evidence for them.

The same test with the tuned α: Model 6, re-derived at calibrated alpha. Part of Calibration.

docs.title: ML baseline, stay level (superseded)
docs.text:
Analysis Master 20-07-2026

Sensei asked whether Random Forest or XGBoost could show the best possible result, since these methods can find curved and combined effects by themselves. Both were trained to choose one of three types, using the same 13 inputs as Model 4a, one row per stay, with no combined terms added by hand. They were tested with normal (not grouped) cross-validation.

Model CV accuracy Building Street Open space Logit (final, 11 params) 0.716 ± 0.016 RF 0.734 ± 0.023 0.878 0.584 0.482 RF, class-weighted 0.745 ± 0.019 0.898 0.584 0.476 XGBoost 0.722 ± 0.027 0.846 0.589 0.508 XGBoost, class-weighted 0.717 ± 0.020 0.823 0.605 0.529

"Class-weighted" means the less common types (street, open space) were given more importance during training.

At the time, this looked like room for a small improvement (Random Forest about +2 percentage points; XGBoost about the same as the logit). Every tree model scored 1.000 on its own training data, which means it memorized the data.

Replaced: normal cross-validation lets recordings of the same stop from different phones end up in both training and testing (Grouped cross-validation). The fair comparison turns the ranking around: ML ceiling check, row level. The finding about σ still holds: Sigma in tree importance.

docs.title: ML ceiling check, row level
docs.text:
Analysis Master 23-07-2026

A fair comparison between the simple model and two machine-learning models. Random Forest and XGBoost got exactly the same task as the simple model (one row per stay and candidate), the raw inputs plus the place type, and exactly the same grouped test sets.

Model In-sample CV (grouped) CV building CV street CV open space Logit, Final model 0.729 0.718 ± 0.028 0.893 0.491 0.450 Random Forest 0.751 0.705 ± 0.027 0.945 0.448 0.282 XGBoost 0.830 0.697 ± 0.044 0.895 0.491 0.345

Both tree models win on the training data (in-sample), and both lose on unseen data (CV). Almost the whole difference comes from open space. For street the three models are close, and for building the trees do a little better. So with a fair test, the machine-learning models offer no improvement. This reverses the earlier result in ML baseline, stay level (superseded).

Settings: Random Forest with 400 trees, depth 8, at least 5 rows per leaf. XGBoost with 300 rounds, depth 4, learning rate 0.1. Neither was tuned. The three models agree only in part on which test sets are hard: fold 1 is among the two hardest for all three (Fold difficulty).

The clearest case of Overfitting signature. Which inputs the trees use: Sigma in tree importance. Part of Complexity and transfer.

docs.title: Model 1: base
docs.text:
Analysis Master 21-07-2026

The first and simplest model: the four scores, each with one weight shared by all place types.

\[V_k = w_1 f_\text{distribution} + w_2 f_\text{distance} + w_3 f_\text{temporal} + w_4 f_\text{directional}\]

Tested with two search distances, 10 m and 15 m:

R=10 m R=15 m LL(C) / LL(b) -0.9507 / -0.9998 -1.0212 / -1.0590 ρ² vs LL(C) -0.052 -0.037 Accuracy 0.519 0.512 Building / street / open space 0.573 / 0.103 / 0.775 0.578 / 0.049 / 0.775 CV accuracy (grouped) 0.522 ± 0.055 0.505 ± 0.065 Condition number 86 78 Term (R=10 m) w t VIF f_distribution +4.261 4.88 21.65 f_distance -0.518 -1.31 3.19 f_temporal -1.281 -1.53 21.43 f_directional -1.391 -4.91 2.21
  • Worse than a simple baseline. ρ² is negative, so this model does worse than just knowing how common each type is. No value of α fixes this: for every α from 0.2 to 6, LL(b) stays between -1.001 and -0.996, below LL(C) (Alpha calibration).
  • f_distribution is significant at both distances. f_temporal is not, and it moves almost the same way as f_distribution (r ≈ 0.96), so it was removed.
  • f_directional is significant at both distances, but with a negative weight. It turns positive once share_type and σ are added (Model 2: share-type and sigma).
  • f_distance has a negative weight at 10 m (-0.52) and a positive one at 15 m (+0.72). This had to wait until α was tuned.
  • The condition number is low, so the fit itself is stable. The problem is which inputs the model has, not the fitting.

Next: Model 2: share-type and sigma. Part of Calibration.

Linked from Alpha calibration · Calibration · MNL model development · Model 2: share-type and sigma · Model progression · R_buffer: 10 m vs 15 m · f_distance · f_distribution · f_temporal

docs.title: Model 2: share-type and sigma
docs.text:
Analysis Master 21-07-2026

The second model removes f_temporal. It adds share_type, with a separate weight for each type, and one sigma term:

\[V_k = w_1 f_\text{distribution} + w_2 f_\text{distance} + w_3 f_\text{directional} + w_4\,share_\text{bldg} + w_5\,share_\text{street} + w_6\,share_\text{os} + w_7\,\sigma\] R=10 m R=15 m ρ² vs LL(C) 0.216 0.219 Accuracy 0.663 0.639 Building / street / open space 0.838 / 0.438 / 0.393 0.838 / 0.405 / 0.314 CV accuracy (grouped) 0.655 ± 0.029 0.642 ± 0.031 Condition number 114 106 Term (R=10 m) w t f_distribution +3.546 8.83 f_distance -1.072 -2.36 f_directional +3.296 8.42 share_bldg +0.936 2.79 share_street -7.292 -16.35 share_os -5.408 -11.59 sigma +0.481 5.92
  • The model now beats the simple baseline, and accuracy is 14 percentage points higher than Model 1: base.
  • The gain is for buildings and streets. Building accuracy rises from 0.57 to 0.84 and street from 0.10 to 0.44, but open space falls from 0.77 to 0.39. The large negative weights share_street and share_os push the probability toward buildings. This is an early sign of Candidate density bias toward building.
  • sigma has a clear positive effect. f_directional turns positive and strongly significant once f_temporal is removed.
  • The weight of f_distance now changes sign between 10 m and 15 m (-1.07 and +1.06), and both values are significant.

Next: Directional scope ablation (3a vs 3b). Part of Calibration.

Linked from Calibration · Directional scope ablation (3a vs 3b) · MNL model development · Model 1: base · Model progression · R_buffer: 10 m vs 15 m · f_distance · share_type · sigma

docs.title: Model 4a: alternative-specific parameters
docs.text:
Analysis Master 21-07-2026

In this model, every score gets its own weight for each place type (building, street, open space). This is called "alternative-specific". sigma keeps one shared weight. In total, 13 parameters:

\[V_t = w_{1,t} f_\text{distribution} + w_{2,t} f_\text{distance} + w_{3,t} f_\text{directional} + w_{4,t}\,share_t + w_5\,\sigma\] Model 4a (R=10 m, α=1) ρ² vs LL(C) 0.292 LR vs 3a (df=6) 131.36, p < 1e-16 Accuracy 0.714 Building / street / open space 0.872 / 0.514 / 0.471 CV accuracy (grouped) 0.697 ± 0.026 Condition number 739

The LR test compares this model with model 3a, which has shared weights. The result is very clear (p < 1e-16): separate weights per type fit much better.

For the first time, all three types improve together (building +3.4 percentage points, street +7.6, open space +7.8). The highest VIF is 8.94, for f_directional_street. The strong overlap between inputs of the same type is explained in Multicollinearity is structural.

f_distance_bldg and f_distance_street are not significant on their own (t = 1.95 and -0.57). Once weights are split by type, part of the distance information is picked up by share and sigma.

All later models build on this one. Next: Model 5: alternative-specific constants (rejected), Interaction term screen (α = 1). α was tuned on this model: Alpha calibration. Part of Calibration.

Linked from Calibration · Directional scope ablation (3a vs 3b) · Interaction term screen (α = 1) · MNL model development · Model 5: alternative-specific constants (rejected) · Model 6, re-derived at calibrated alpha · Model progression · Multicollinearity is structural

docs.title: Model 5: alternative-specific constants (rejected)
docs.text:
Analysis Master 21-07-2026

Model 4a: alternative-specific parameters plus two constants, asc_street and asc_os. A constant (ASC) is a fixed extra value for each type, which shows whether a type is preferred in general. Building is the reference (\(ASC_\text{bldg} = 0\)). In total, 15 parameters:

\[V_t = w_{1,t} f_\text{distribution} + w_{2,t} f_\text{distance} + w_{3,t} f_\text{directional} + w_{4,t}\,share_t + w_5\,\sigma + ASC_t\] 4a 5 (+ ASC) Accuracy 0.714 0.728 CV accuracy (grouped) 0.697 ± 0.026 0.719 ± 0.016 LR vs 4a (df=2) 44.7, p < 0.0001 Max VIF 8.94 31.04 Condition number 739 2,055

On paper, the constants are significant, and accuracy on unseen data also goes up (by a little less than the normal spread between test sets of Model 4a). But asc_street and f_directional_street move almost together (r = 0.94). The reason: f_directional hardly changes between street candidates, so it acts almost like a constant for streets. The model is asked to measure the same "street-ness" twice. As a result, the weight of the street direction score changes sign, from +3.59 in Model 4a to -5.23, so the two weights can no longer be read on their own.

With the tuned α it gets worse: each constant also moves almost together with its own f_distance score (asc_t and f_distance_t, r = 0.99), and the highest VIF rises to 116. With a 15 m search distance the model behaves about the same as at 10 m (accuracy on unseen data 0.707 ± 0.019, condition number 1,844).

Rejected, because its weights cannot be trusted. It is not a case of overfitting: the gain on unseen data is real, but it comes from a near-copy of another input (Overfitting signature). Part of Calibration.

docs.title: Model 6, re-derived at calibrated alpha
docs.text:
Analysis Master 21-07-2026

Model 6 built again with the tuned α (2.979). It starts from Model 4a: alternative-specific parameters and adds the two terms that still passed the test with the new α: σ² and f_distribution × share_type. In total, 15 parameters:

\[V_t = w_{1,t} f_\text{distribution} + w_{2,t} f_\text{distance} + w_{3,t} f_\text{directional} + w_{4,t}\,share_t + w_5\,\sigma + w_6\,\sigma^2 + w_7\,(f_\text{distribution}\times share_\text{type})\] 4a at α* Model 6 re-derived LL(b) -0.6453 -0.6355 LR vs 4a at α* (df=2) 17.73, p < 0.001 Accuracy 0.727 0.722 CV accuracy (grouped) 0.710 ± 0.030 0.698 ± 0.043 Condition number 2,036 11,696 Max VIF 25.85 (f_distance, street) 36.70 (σ)

The fit is significantly better, but accuracy drops a little, also on unseen data, and the model becomes much less stable (condition number from 2,036 to 11,696). σ² again adds little (t = 0.15). Next: Stepwise VIF elimination. Part of Calibration.

docs.text:
Analysis Master 21-07-2026

All models in one table, in the order they were built. Every model was tested with Grouped cross-validation, with a 10 m search distance unless the row says 15 m.

How to read it: Accuracy is measured on the training data. CV accuracy is measured on unseen data and is the fairer number. Condition number shows how stable the model is: higher means less stable.

Model α Params Accuracy CV accuracy (grouped) Condition no. Model 1: base 1 4 0.519 0.522 ± 0.055 86 Model 1: base, 15 m 1 4 0.512 0.505 ± 0.065 78 Model 2: share-type and sigma 1 7 0.663 0.655 ± 0.029 114 Model 2: share-type and sigma, 15 m 1 7 0.639 0.642 ± 0.031 106 3b, Directional scope ablation (3a vs 3b) 1 7 0.653 0.644 ± 0.023 231 Model 4a: alternative-specific parameters 1 13 0.714 0.697 ± 0.026 739 Model 5: alternative-specific constants (rejected) 1 15 0.728 0.719 ± 0.016 2,055 Model 6, Interaction term screen (α = 1) 1 16 0.716 0.709 ± 0.037 13,815 Model 4a at α* 2.98 13 0.727 0.710 ± 0.030 2,036 Model 6, re-derived at calibrated alpha 2.98 15 0.722 0.698 ± 0.043 11,696 Stepwise VIF elimination 2.98 13 0.727 0.710 ± 0.030 2,036 Final model 2.98 11 0.729 0.718 ± 0.028 1,869

docs.title: R_buffer: 10 m vs 15 m
docs.text:
Analysis Master 19-07-2026

Which search distance (R_buffer) is better for finding candidates around a stay? 10 m beats 15 m for every model tested, in accuracy and in fit (log-likelihood). Stability does not decide it: the condition number is lower at 15 m for some models and at 10 m for others.

Model Accuracy R=10 m Accuracy R=15 m Δ 1 Base 0.519 0.512 +0.8 pp 2 Share-type + σ 0.663 0.639 +2.3 pp 4a Alternative-specific 0.714 0.691 +2.3 pp 5 + ASC 0.728 0.726 +0.2 pp 6 + interactions 0.716 0.699 +1.7 pp

(pp = percentage points.) The result held again with Grouped cross-validation on 21-07-2026. From the directional test onward, only 10 m was used.

One caution: ρ² cannot be compared between the two distances, because its baseline changes when the candidates change (Model evaluation metrics).

A wider search distance brings in more street pieces that are not really relevant. Street accuracy suffers at 15 m (Model 1: base, Model 2: share-type and sigma).

docs.text:
Analysis Master 29-07-2026

How the fit changes with α, for the downsampled data and for the full data. Same method as in Alpha calibration, using Model 4a. LL(b) closer to 0 means a better fit.

α Downsampled LL(b) Raw-density LL(b) 1.0 -0.6731 -0.7154 2.0 -0.6494 -0.6913 2.979 -0.6453 3.0 -0.6453 -0.6855 4.0 -0.6461 -0.6828 5.0 -0.6447 -0.6812 6.0 -0.6437 -0.6804

With downsampled data, the fit has an inside best point at α = 2.979. It is almost flat above α ≈ 2.4, and it rises slowly again above α ≈ 4 (at α = 6 it is higher by 1.4 total log-likelihood units, which is not significant). docs.title: Raw-density refit
docs.text:
Analysis Master 29-07-2026

Sensei asked whether downsampling the survey data (Downsampling to MILES density) changes the result. To check, the Final model was fitted again on the same 907 stays, using the full data (152,602 points instead of 15,687). The search distance, the score formulas, the 11-parameter form and the test sets stayed the same. α and sigma_scale were tuned again for the full data.

Downsampled Raw density Calibrated α 2.979 6.000 (search limit) Candidate rows 20,219 32,563 Accuracy 0.729 0.714 CV accuracy (grouped) 0.718 ± 0.028 0.709 ± 0.032 Condition number 1,869 4,735

Downsampling does no harm. The downsampled version is slightly more accurate on unseen data (0.718 against 0.709) and much more stable. All 11 weights keep the same sign (positive or negative). The f_distance weights are larger with the full data (street 2.3 times, open space 1.8 times; the building weight is small and not significant in the downsampled model). That follows from the larger α, because the distance score changes with α, so it does not mean the two models disagree.

More results from this test: Raw-density alpha profile, Downsampling shrinks the candidate search area. Part of Complexity and transfer.

docs.title: Sigma in tree importance
docs.text:
Analysis Master 23-07-2026

sigma (how spread out a stay's GPS points are) has a moderate weight in the simple model (+1.05 in the Final model). But the tree models rank it as one of their most important inputs:

Run σ rank Stay-level, RF impurity / XGBoost gain 1st / 1st Stay-level, out-of-fold permutation RF 1st, XGBoost 4th Row-level, RF impurity 1st (0.35) Row-level, XGBoost gain 3rd, after the building and street indicators

(Impurity, gain and permutation are three common ways to measure how much a tree model uses an input.)

There are two possible explanations:

  • σ may work like a threshold: below some spread one answer is likely, above it another. One straight-line weight cannot show that.
  • The trees may use σ as a stand-in for something related to it, such as how long the stay lasted or the surroundings.

σ² did not survive in the simple model (Stepwise VIF elimination). Other forms, such as log(σ) or a threshold, have not been tried yet.

In the row-level test, the trees learn the differences between types directly from the place-type input. f_distance ranks last in both tree models.

Sources: ML baseline, stay level (superseded), ML ceiling check, row level. Part of Complexity and transfer.

Linked from Complexity and transfer · ML baseline · ML baseline, stay level (superseded) · ML ceiling check, row level · sigma

docs.title: Stepwise VIF elimination
docs.text:
Analysis Master 21-07-2026

Removing weak terms one at a time from Model 6, re-derived at calibrated alpha. At each step, find the extra term (not one of the core terms) with the highest VIF, remove it, and fit the model again. Stop when every extra term has a VIF of 10 or less. The 13 core terms from Model 4a are never removed (Multicollinearity is structural).

Step Worst droppable VIF Action 0 σ² 19.54 drop 1 f_distribution × share_type 10.71 drop 2 none left stop

Both extra terms go. f_distribution × share_type is only just above the line of 10, although it is significant on its own (t = 4.77 before the first step). Removing both costs some fit (LR = 17.73, df = 2, p < 0.001), but accuracy on unseen data goes up (0.698 → 0.710), and the condition number drops about 6 times (11,696 → 2,036), so the model becomes much more stable.

Result, the 13-parameter model: the 13 core terms of Model 4a, at α = 2.979.

\[V_t = w_{1,t} f_\text{distribution} + w_{2,t} f_\text{distance} + w_{3,t} f_\text{directional} + w_{4,t}\,share_t + w_5\,\sigma\]

Accuracy 0.727, accuracy on unseen data 0.710 ± 0.030, condition number 2,036.

Later it was made smaller, to 11 parameters: f_directional: shared vs split. Part of Calibration.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
Concept 05-08-2026

Plain explanations of the words that come back in many notes. Each note also explains its own terms the first time it uses them.

docs.title: Places and data
docs.text:
Stay cluster (stay). A group of GPS points recorded while a person stayed in one place, for example sitting in a cafe for 20 minutes.

Entity. One place on the map: a building, a street, or an open space (a park, a plaza).

Entity type. Building, street or open space. The model predicts the type of place, not the exact building.

Candidate. An entity close enough to a stay to be a possible answer. Each stay has a list of candidates.

Ground truth (GT). The correct answers. In this study, participants wrote down where they really were, so each stay has a known correct type.

MILES. A large GPS dataset from a smartphone app. The model is meant to be used on MILES later.

docs.title: Model terms
docs.text:
Model. A formula that turns the scores of each candidate into a probability for building, street and open space.

MNL / logit / conditional logit. The type of model used here. It gives each candidate a value, and turns those values into probabilities that add up to 1.

Weight (coefficient, w). How much one score counts in the model. The model learns the weights from the ground truth.

Parameter. A number the model learns. "11 parameters" means the model learns 11 weights.

Generic vs alternative-specific. A generic weight is the same for all three types. An alternative-specific weight is different for building, street and open space.

ASC (alternative-specific constant). A fixed extra value for each type, used to see if one type is preferred in general.

Calibration. Finding the best weights and settings by fitting the model to the ground truth.

α (alpha). A setting that controls how fast the distance score drops as a candidate gets farther away.

σ (sigma). How spread out the GPS points of a stay are. A large σ means the GPS position was uncertain.

R_buffer. The search distance around each GPS point. Entities inside this distance become candidates. The study uses 10 m.

docs.title: How results are measured
docs.text:
Accuracy. The share of stays where the model's top answer is the correct type. 0.718 means 71.8% correct.

Recall (per type). Of all stays that really were, for example, street, the share the model called street.

In-sample. Accuracy measured on the same data the model learned from. It is usually too optimistic.

Cross-validation (CV). The data is split into 5 parts (folds). The model learns from 4 parts and is tested on the 5th, five times. This shows how well the model works on data it has not seen.

Grouped CV. CV where all recordings of the same stop stay in the same part. This study needs it because several phones (three for most stops) recorded each stop at the same time.

± value. How much the result changes from fold to fold (one standard deviation). In 0.718 ± 0.028, the 0.028 shows that some folds are easier than others.

Log-likelihood (LL). A number that shows how well the model's probabilities fit the correct answers. Closer to 0 is better.

ρ² (rho-squared). How much better the model is than a simple baseline. Negative means worse than the baseline.

t-value. How clearly a weight differs from zero. Above about 2 (or below -2) usually counts as significant.

p-value. The chance of seeing a result this strong if there were no real effect. Below 0.05 usually counts as significant.

LR test (likelihood-ratio test). A test that checks whether extra parameters improve the fit enough to be worth keeping.

Overfitting. When a model learns the training data too closely, including noise, and then does worse on new data.

docs.title: Warning signs in a model
docs.text:
Correlation (r). How closely two numbers move together, from -1 to 1. Near 1 means they almost always rise and fall together.

Multicollinearity. When several scores in a model are strongly correlated, so the model cannot tell their effects apart well.

VIF (variance inflation factor). A number for each score that shows multicollinearity. Above 10 is the usual warning line.

Condition number. One number for the whole model that shows how stable the fit is. Large values (thousands) mean the individual weights are unreliable.

Random Forest, XGBoost. Two machine-learning methods built from many decision trees. They are flexible but hard to interpret.

Part of Thesis summary.

Linked from MNL model development · Model evaluation metrics · Thesis summary

docs.title: Candidate density as boundary-matching difficulty
docs.text:
Concept Master 23-07-2026

GPS research on roads and sidewalks knows a similar problem. Weng et al. (2025) need a special sidewalk-matching method, because a sidewalk is only about 2 m wide, while GPS error between tall buildings reaches 18.4 m (RMS) when standing and up to 32 m across the street when walking. Quddus et al. (2007) report three related problems: point-to-line matching becomes unstable when roads are close together, one matching method gets worse on parallel streets, and at a Y-shaped junction both roads can be almost equally close.

Candidate density bias toward building is a similar problem at a larger scale. When many candidates of the same type are packed close together, a small GPS error has more chances to land on a wrong one.

The comparison has a limit. Those papers choose between places of the same kind, for example two roads. Here, the problem is a competition between types: streets lose to buildings. The two problems share one cause, candidates packed close together, but they work in different ways.

A subsection of the Discussion in the thesis. Part of Error analysis.

Linked from Candidate density bias toward building · Error analysis

docs.title: Candidate selection
docs.text:
Concept Master 25-07-2026

How the method decides which places to consider for one stay. Draw a circle with radius R_buffer around every GPS point of the stay. Every place that touches at least one circle becomes a candidate:

\[\text{Candidates}(C_i) = \{E_k \mid \min_{p \in C_i} d(p, E_k) \leq R_\text{buffer}\}\]

In words: place \(E_k\) is a candidate if its distance \(d\) to at least one point \(p\) of stay \(C_i\) is at most \(R_\text{buffer}\).

A circle is used instead of "the point is inside the place", because GPS error can put a recorded point outside the place where the person really was. f_distribution uses the same radius on purpose.

R_buffer = 10 m was chosen over 15 m: R_buffer: 10 m vs 15 m. Because each point has its own circle, a stay with more points covers a larger area: Downsampling shrinks the candidate search area.

Part of Framework overview.

Linked from Assignment framework · CEUS paper revisions · Downsampling shrinks the candidate search area · Framework overview · R_buffer: 10 m vs 15 m

docs.title: Contributions
docs.text:
Concept Master 25-07-2026

What is new in this thesis.

  1. A new method. It is the first method that gives a stay a probability for three types of place (building, street, open space) instead of one fixed answer. It works for people standing still, and it learns its weights from data instead of using fixed values (Framework overview, Final model).
  2. New data and a new finding. A cleaned set of 907 stays in Hiroshima with known correct answers (Ground truth dataset). And the finding that streets score lower because of how the street map is cut into pieces, which can be fixed. The GPS data itself is not the limit (Candidate density bias toward building).

docs.title: Downsampling to MILES density
docs.text:
Concept Master 25-07-2026

The survey phones recorded a GPS point about every metre. MILES records far fewer points. If the model learned from the dense survey data, it would not fit MILES well. So before scoring, the survey data is downsampled to the typical MILES density of 0.967 points per minute.

For a stay that lasts \(d\) minutes, the number of points to keep is

\[n = \max\big(1,\ \mathrm{round}(d \times 0.967)\big)\]

but never more than the stay originally had. The first and the last point are always kept. The other \(n - 2\) points are picked at random from the points in between, and no point is picked twice.

For the 907 stays, this leaves 15,687 points out of the original 152,602, about 9.7 times fewer. Only the choice of points is random: the number of points per stay follows from its length.

Does downsampling change the result? A test with the full data says no: Raw-density refit. Downsampling also makes the search area around each stay smaller: Downsampling shrinks the candidate search area.

Part of Ground truth data.

docs.title: Experiment design
docs.text:
Concept Master 25-07-2026

The correct answers (ground truth) come from a planned field survey. Participants visited places with set instructions and wrote down where they were.

  • 11 participants, each doing 2 sessions, between 5 and 14 June 2026.
  • 5 groups of stops (A to E), each testing one theme. Each session has 12 planned stops and 4 free stops chosen by the participant: Group A: vertical position (floor level), Group B: sky view obstruction (how much sky is visible), Group C: indoor position (position inside a building), Group D: movement type (how the person moves), Group E: ambiguous edge cases (places that are hard to classify).
  • 3 phones per session (4 or 5 in six sessions), to collect more GPS data. The recordings of one stop are not independent of each other. This is why testing uses Grouped cross-validation.
  • The start and end of each stay come from the Self-report form, not from an algorithm.

Result: Ground truth dataset. Part of Ground truth data.

docs.title: Group A: vertical position
docs.text:

docs.title: f_directional
docs.text:
Concept Master 25-07-2026

Does the person's small movement during the stay follow the direction of a street? Someone standing on a street often moves along it. Someone inside a building moves in more random directions.

For a street candidate, the score is high when the movement follows that street:

\[f_\text{directional}(E_k, C_i) = \frac{1}{|J|} \sum_{j \in J} |\cos(\theta_j - \theta_{E_k})|\]

For a building or open-space candidate, movement along a nearby street counts against it. The score is 1 minus the best match with any nearby street, so every candidate gets a value:

\[f_\text{directional}(E_k, C_i) = 1 - \max_{s \in \text{Adjacent}(E_k)} \left\{ \frac{1}{|J|} \sum_{j \in J} |\cos(\theta_j - \theta_s)| \right\}\]

\(\theta_j\) is the direction from point \(j\) to point \(j+1\). \(J\) is the set of steps longer than 0.5 m; shorter steps are left out to ignore GPS noise. \(\theta_{E_k}\) is the direction of the street, taken from its centre line: the average direction of the line's pieces, weighted by their length, where a direction and its reverse count as the same. \(\text{Adjacent}(E_k)\) means the street pieces within 30 m. If no step is longer than 0.5 m, or a building or open space has no street within 30 m, the score is a neutral 0.5.

In the models: finding the right form took three tests: Directional scope ablation (3a vs 3b), its overlap with the ASC terms in Model 5: alternative-specific constants (rejected), and finally f_directional: shared vs split. The final answer is one weight shared by all three place types.

Part of Framework overview.

Linked from Assignment framework · CEUS paper revisions · Directional scope ablation (3a vs 3b) · Framework overview · Model 1: base · Model 2: share-type and sigma · Model 5: alternative-specific constants (rejected) · f_directional: shared vs split

docs.title: f_distance
docs.text:
Concept Master 25-07-2026

How close the candidate is to the center of the stay. The score is 1 when the candidate is at the center and falls toward 0 as it gets farther away. How fast it falls depends on how spread out the stay's points are (\(\sigma_i\)) and on a setting \(\alpha\):

\[f_{\text{distance}}(E_k, C_i) = \exp\left(-\frac{d_{ki}^2}{2(\alpha \cdot \sigma_i)^2}\right)\]

\(d_{ki}\) is the distance from the stay's medoid to candidate \(E_k\), and 0 when the medoid lies inside it. The medoid is the GPS point closest to the average position of the stay. \(\sigma_i\) is the spread of the stay's points (sigma), with a minimum of 5 m. When the points are widely spread, the GPS position is less certain, so the score falls more slowly and farther places still get some credit.

In the models: \(\alpha\) was 1.0 (not tuned) until Alpha calibration set it to 2.979. Before that, its weight changed sign between the 10 m and 15 m search distances (Model 1: base, Model 2: share-type and sigma). A squared version of this score also looked useful, but only because α was wrong (The f_distance² artifact).

Part of Framework overview.

Linked from Alpha calibration · Assignment framework · CEUS paper revisions · Framework overview · Model 1: base · Model 2: share-type and sigma · sigma

docs.title: f_distribution
docs.text:
Concept Master 25-07-2026

The share of the stay's time spent near the candidate. It counts the GPS points within R_buffer of the candidate, weighted by time:

\[f_\text{distribution}(E_k, C_i) = \frac{\sum_{p \in C_i} W_p \cdot \mathbf{1}\{d(p, E_k) \leq R_\text{buffer}\}}{\sum_{p \in C_i} W_p}\]

\(\mathbf{1}\{\dots\}\) is 1 when point \(p\) is close enough to the candidate and 0 otherwise. \(W_p\) is the time weight of point \(p\) (following Wu et al., 2026). Phones do not record points at even time steps, so each point gets a weight equal to the time it stands for. Points in the middle get \(W_p = (t_{p+1} - t_{p-1})/2\), half the time between the point before and the point after. The first and last points get:

\[W_1 = \frac{t_1 + t_2}{2}, \qquad W_n = 1 - \frac{t_{n-1} + t_n}{2}\]

Here the times of one stay are rescaled to run from 0 to 1 (\(t_1 = 0\), \(t_n = 1\)), so the weights of a stay add up to 1. A stay with a single point gives that point the weight 1.

In the models: this score was significant from the very first model (Model 1: base), and it is the strongest open-space term in the Final model. Its product with share_type passed the screen of combined terms (Interaction term screen (α = 1)), but the overlap check removed it, so the final model has no combined term (Stepwise VIF elimination).

Part of Framework overview.

Linked from Assignment framework · CEUS paper revisions · Candidate selection · Framework overview · Model 1: base · f_temporal

docs.title: f_temporal
docs.text:
Concept Master 25-07-2026

The longest unbroken stretch of time the stay spent at the candidate, as a share of the whole stay:

\[f_\text{temporal}(E_k, C_i) = \frac{\max_{S \in S(E_k, C_i)} \sum_{p \in S} W_p}{\sum_{p \in C_i} W_p}\]

\(S\) is a run of points in time order that belong to candidate \(E_k\). A point belongs to \(E_k\) when it lies within R_buffer (10 m) of it, as in f_distribution. \(W_p\) is the time weight from f_distribution. The score takes the longest run.

A short jump outside does not end a run. A point more than 10 m away still counts toward the run when it comes at most \(\Delta t_\text{gap} = 300\) seconds after the last point within 10 m. The run ends only at a point outside that comes more than five minutes after the last point within 10 m. A stretch with no GPS points at all never ends a run, because missing points give no sign that the person left.

Example: a 60-minute stay is within 10 m from minute 0 to 20, outside for 3 minutes, back from 23 to 40, outside for 10 minutes, and back from 50 to 60. The first run covers minutes 0 to 40, so \(f_\text{temporal}\) = 40/60 ≈ 0.67.

In the models: this score was removed after the first model. It was never significant, and it moved almost the same way as f_distribution (correlation r ≈ 0.96, VIF about 22), so it added little new information. See Model 1: base.

Part of Framework overview.

Linked from Assignment framework · CEUS paper revisions · Framework overview · Model 1: base · Model 2: share-type and sigma

docs.title: Framework overview
docs.text:
Concept Master 25-07-2026

The method in four steps, from one stay to a probability for each type of place.

  1. Candidates. Find every place (building, street piece or open space) within R_buffer of the stay's GPS points (Candidate selection).
  2. Scores. Give each candidate four scores, each looking at the GPS points in a different way: f_distribution, f_distance, f_temporal, f_directional.
  3. Utility. Add the scores together, each multiplied by a weight. The result \(V_k\) (the "utility") says how likely candidate \(k\) is. Calibration later added two more inputs, share_type and sigma.
\[V_k = w_1 f_\text{distribution} + w_2 f_\text{distance} + w_3 f_\text{temporal} + w_4 f_\text{directional}\]

The scores are added, not multiplied. With multiplication, one score of zero would remove a candidate, even if its other scores were high. 4. Probability. Turn the utilities into probabilities for each type \(t\) (building, street, open space). The model adds up \(\exp(V_k)\) for all candidates of that type and divides by the total for all candidates. This is a conditional logit model.

\[P(t \mid C_i) = \frac{\sum_{k \in t} \exp(V_k)}{\sum_{j \in \text{Candidates}(C_i)} \exp(V_j)}\]

The weights \(w\) are not chosen by hand. The model learns them from the Ground truth dataset, by finding the weights that best predict the correct answers (maximum likelihood).

Part of Assignment framework. Answers the "how" part of Research questions RQ1.

Concept Master 23-07-2026

How the survey records were cleaned before use, as written in the final thesis (Section 3.3.4).

First, the self-report forms were checked against the GPS tracks:

  • Four entries had a typo in one time field (one hour or twelve hours off). Each was corrected using the stops before and after, the time the form was sent, and the GPS track.

docs.title: Grouped cross-validation
docs.text:
Concept Master 21-07-2026

Cross-validation (CV) tests a model on data it did not learn from. The data is split into 5 parts. The model learns from 4 parts and is tested on the 5th, and this repeats five times.

In this survey, several phones recorded each stop at the same time: three for most stops, up to five (Experiment design). So up to five records share the same correct answer and the same situation. In normal CV, one phone's record can land in the training part and another phone's record of the same stop in the test part. The model then sees almost the same stop during learning and testing, and the result looks better than it should.

Since 21-07-2026, every CV number uses StratifiedGroupKFold with 5 parts, grouped by real stop (participant and stop number). All records of one stop always stay in the same part. All models were tested again this way (Model progression).

The effect, shown on the final 11-parameter model: normal CV gives 0.716 ± 0.016, grouped CV gives 0.718 ± 0.028. The average barely moves, but the range is almost twice as wide. The wider range is the honest one. Earlier results from normal CV, such as ML baseline, stay level (superseded), are replaced.

Part of Calibration.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
Concept Master 25-07-2026

What the results of this thesis cannot show.

  • Planned behaviour. Participants followed instructions, so their behaviour was not fully natural. This matters most for the stops with small movements (Group D: movement type).
  • Several phones per stop. The recordings of one stop (three for most stops, up to five) are not independent. Grouped cross-validation reduces this problem but does not remove it.
  • Terraces and balconies. "Building-attached Outdoor" is counted as open space (Self-report form).
  • One street map. The street results come partly from how this map cuts streets into pieces, so the street numbers belong to this map (Candidate density bias toward building).
  • Open-space errors. The cause of the open-space errors has not been found.
  • Stays one by one. Each stay is judged alone, without the trips before and after it.
  • No MILES test yet. The model has not been used on MILES, so the risk described in Overfitting signature has not been tested.

docs.title: Extending map matching to stationary stays
docs.text:
Concept Master 23-07-2026

Map matching finds which road a moving person is on. Bierlaire et al. (2013), Chen and Bierlaire (2015) and Kempinska et al. (2016) all give probabilities, and they all build them from a chain of points: each point depends on the point before it, or the method steps forward through time (a Markov chain or a particle filter). A person standing still has no chain. There is no earlier point on a route, no previous step and no next road piece.

One idea still works: keep several possible places, each with a probability. The way of computing those probabilities has to change. This method uses only what one stay shows by itself: how its points spread, how long they stay, and how they move (Framework overview).

Quddus et al. (2007) support this change. They note that matching point by point, without the track history, often picks the wrong road. They also name places off the road network, such as car parks, as a problem that map matching has not solved.

A subsection of the Discussion in the thesis. Part of Problem and positioning. The starting point: Motivation.

docs.title: Motivation
docs.text:
Concept Master 25-07-2026

Why the usual way of linking GPS stays to places is not good enough.

The usual way is deterministic: it gives one fixed answer. Each stay goes to the nearest building, or to the building that contains the GPS points. This has two problems:

  1. Streets and open spaces are left out. People also spend time on streets, in parks and in plazas. Urban researchers such as Jacobs, Gehl and Whyte describe these places as real sites of daily life (Tension with the street-space argument).
  2. GPS error is ignored. The method forces one answer, even when the GPS position is uncertain and two or three places are equally possible.

Probabilistic methods already exist for people who are moving. These methods (called map matching) give probabilities for which road a moving person is on. But nobody had used this idea for a person who stays in one place. And nobody had combined it with all three place types: building, street and open space (Extending map matching to stationary stays).

This leads to the Research questions. Part of Problem and positioning.

docs.title: Multicollinearity is structural
docs.text:
Concept Master 19-07-2026

Why some warning numbers (VIF above 10) are expected in this model and are not a mistake.

When each type gets its own weights, the inputs for one type (f_distance_t, f_directional_t, share_t) all come from the same list of candidates of that stay. So they move together closely (correlation often r = 0.8-0.93). This overlap is called multicollinearity, and it raises the VIF of important terms above 10.

The overlap comes from how the model is built. It does not mean some inputs are useless copies. To push every VIF below 10, some of these separate weights would have to go, and they are the reason this model works better than the simpler ones (Model 4a: alternative-specific parameters). So when weak terms were removed step by step, these important terms were protected (Stepwise VIF elimination).

One kind of overlap is a real problem: an ASC term (a fixed extra value per type) that copies an input which barely changes within its type (Model 5: alternative-specific constants (rejected)).

Visible in Final model correlation matrix. Part of Calibration.

docs.title: Overfitting signature
docs.text:
Concept Master 25-07-2026

Again and again, a more complex model fit the training data better without doing better on unseen data. That is the sign of overfitting: the model learns details of this sample that do not carry over. Three cases:

  1. Adding σ² and f_distribution × share_type at the tuned α: Stepwise VIF elimination
  2. Giving f_directional a separate weight per type: f_directional: shared vs split
  3. The squared distance term, before α was tuned: The f_distance² artifact

One step does not fit this pattern. The ASC terms (a fixed extra value per type) also raised accuracy on unseen data. They were rejected because they copy another input, not because of overfitting (Model 5: alternative-specific constants (rejected)).

The tree models show the same thing on a bigger scale. Both beat the simple model on the training data and lose to it on unseen data (ML ceiling check, row level).

Why this matters for MILES: the survey's mix of 59% building, 20% street and 21% open space was set by the survey plan (Ground truth dataset). The share_type weights learned patterns of this sample. MILES may have a different mix, so it is not yet known how well the model will work there (Limitations).

Answers Research questions RQ3. Part of Complexity and transfer.

docs.title: Positioning against deterministic assignment
docs.text:
Concept Master 23-07-2026

How this method differs from methods that give one fixed answer (deterministic methods).

Chapter 2 describes two of them. SMoT checks whether part of a GPS track stays inside a place's outline for a minimum time (Alvares et al., 2007). Wu et al. (2026) give each GPS point to its nearest place. Both choose one place and say nothing about how sure they are.

Wu et al. do calculate the chance of a wrong answer. That chance depends on the GPS error and on how close the point is to the edge of a place. But they only use it afterwards, to report accuracy. This method builds the same idea into the answer itself: it gives a probability for each type. Its accuracy on unseen data is 0.718 ± 0.028 (Final model).

Would a more flexible model do better? Research question 3 says no. Random Forest and XGBoost fit the training data better (0.751 and 0.830, against 0.729), but they do worse on unseen data (0.705 and 0.697, against 0.718) (ML ceiling check, row level). The simple model has the right amount of complexity for this data. And anyone can read it: it is just eleven weights, each with a clear sign.

docs.title: share_type
docs.text:
Concept Master 19-07-2026

How common the candidate's own type is among all candidates of the stay. If a stay has 20 candidates and 12 of them are street pieces, the street share is 12/20 = 0.6. With \(n_{t,i}\) candidates of type \(t\) out of \(N_i\) candidates for stay \(i\):

\[\text{share}_t(C_i) = \frac{n_{t,i}}{N_i}\]

Each type gets its own weight (share_bldg, share_street, share_os). Each column holds the share for rows of that type and 0 for the other rows.

In the models: adding this term fixed the biggest problem of the first model (Model 2: share-type and sigma). But its weight for street is large and negative (-5.16 in the Final model; for open space it is +0.25 and not significant). So a street candidate with many neighbouring street pieces gets a lower value. That is the cause of the street errors in Candidate density bias toward building.

Part of Assignment framework.

docs.title: sigma
docs.text:
Concept Master 19-07-2026

How spread out the GPS points of one stay are. A large σ means the points are scattered, so the GPS position was uncertain.

\[\sigma_i = \sqrt{\mathrm{var}(x) + \mathrm{var}(y)}\]

\(\mathrm{var}(x)\) and \(\mathrm{var}(y)\) are the variances of the east-west and north-south positions.

σ is used in two places:

  • Inside f_distance it sets how fast the distance score falls, with a minimum of 5 m.
  • As its own model input. Very large values are capped at 165.04 m (the 99th percentile). Then the value is divided by sigma_scale = 34.862, the standard deviation of the capped values. This scale is computed once and reused unchanged in every model:
\[\sigma_k = \begin{cases} \min(\sigma_i,\ 165.04) \,/\, 34.862 & \text{street or open-space candidate} \\ 0 & \text{building candidate} \end{cases}\]

σ gets one weight shared by all types, with building as the reference (0 for building rows). σ has the same value for all candidates of a stay. Giving it a separate weight per type would make the model unable to tell the weights apart, so that option is not available.

In the models: σ has a clear positive effect in every model (Model 2: share-type and sigma, Final model). Tree models rank it much higher than its moderate weight suggests: Sigma in tree importance.

Part of Assignment framework.

docs.title: Spatial entity layers
docs.text:
Concept Master 25-07-2026

The map is split into three types of place (entities).

Type Source Building Zmap TOWN building outlines, used as they are Street MAPPLE street center lines, widened to the width of each street Open space All land that is left after streets and buildings are removed from the street network area. Rivers and other water are not part of it.

Open space never overlaps the other two types. Buildings and streets do overlap in places, where a widened street reaches into a building outline, so a GPS point can lie inside both. Both map sources start in the old Tokyo Datum and are converted to JGD2000 with the official TKY2JGD grid, then to one projected system (WGS 84 / UTM zone 53N, EPSG:32653).

Two details matter later:

  • Streets are stored as many short pieces next to each other. Because of this, a stay on a street has many street candidates around it, and this hurts the model: Candidate density bias toward building.
  • Underground shopping arcades are not in Zmap TOWN. Stays recorded there had no matching building, so they were removed: Ground truth drop list.

Part of Ground truth data.

docs.title: Tension with the street-space argument
docs.text:
Concept Master 23-07-2026

The method treats streets and open spaces as places just as important as buildings, because Jacobs, Gehl and Whyte describe them as real sites of daily life. The results of research question 2 make this harder. The model finds 89.3% of building stays, but only 49.2% of street stays and 45.0% of open-space stays, and it mistakes both mostly for buildings (Confusion matrix).

For streets, the cause lies in how the model was fitted, not in weak GPS data. The share_type term gives a lower value to a candidate with many neighbours of the same type. Street stays have about 1.9 times as many same-type candidates as building stays (13.13 against 7.00 on average), because the map stores streets as many short pieces (Candidate density bias toward building). For open space this explanation does not work: open-space stays have the fewest same-type candidates, and the cause of their errors is still open.

For streets, two explanations are still possible:

  • The problem belongs to this street map. A map with fewer, longer street pieces would make the gap smaller.
  • Long, repeated place types like streets are at a disadvantage in any method that counts nearby candidates.

None of the papers checked can decide between the two. Testing other ways of cutting the street map could (Future work).

A subsection of the Discussion in the thesis. Part of Error analysis.

docs.title: Fast marching method
docs.text: Note

docs.title: 1. Executive Summary & Problem Context
docs.text:
In spatial modeling and urban form analysis, converting point or footprint-based parcel representations into realistic influence zones often leads to geometrical degeneracies when using classical Voronoi tessellations: - Submerged Sites: Sites with small weights are completely absorbed by sites with large weights. - Site Eviction: Points are pushed outside their own Voronoi cells. - Topological Leakage / Over-reaching: Unconstrained Euclidean expansion allows massive structures (e.g., shopping malls) to "wrap around" barriers and absorb parcels located behind intervening buildings.

The Fast Marching Method (FMM) resolves these pathologies by reformulating spatial allocation as a boundary-value propagation problem governed by the Eikonal partial differential equation. Building footprints serve as zero-cost initialization interfaces, opposing footprints act as impenetrable obstacles, and the Total Floor Area (TFA) parameterizes the local propagation speed.

docs.title: 2.1 The Eikonal Equation
docs.text:
The evolution of an advancing monotonically moving interface through an \(n\)-dimensional domain \(\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^n\) can be characterized by an arrival time function \(T(x)\), which describes the exact time at which the expanding wavefront crosses position \(x \in \Omega\).

The governing boundary-value problem is the stationary Eikonal Equation:

\[|\nabla T(x)| = \frac{1}{F(x)}, \quad x \in \Omega \setminus \Gamma\] \[\text{subject to} \quad T(x) = 0, \quad x \in \Gamma\]

where: - \(T(x): \Omega \to [0, \infty)\) denotes the arrival time (or geodesic action potential). - \(\nabla T(x) = \left( \frac{\partial T}{\partial x_1}, \dots, \frac{\partial T}{\partial x_n} \right)\) is the spatial gradient vector of the arrival time. - \(F(x) > 0\) is the scalar speed function of the front at point \(x\). - \(f(x) = \frac{1}{F(x)}\) is the slowness or cost function. - \(\Gamma = \bigcup_{i=1}^M \Gamma_i\) represents the initial source boundary consisting of \(M\) discrete interfaces (e.g., building footprint boundaries).

docs.title: 2.2 Geodesic Metric and Characteristics
docs.text:
By the method of characteristics and the calculus of variations (Fermat's Principle), the solution \(T(x)\) to the Eikonal equation corresponds to the minimum travel-time metric:

\[T(x) = \inf_{\gamma \in \mathcal{P}(\Gamma, x)} \int_0^L \frac{1}{F(\gamma(s))} \, ds\]

where \(\mathcal{P}(\Gamma, x)\) is the collection of all rectifiable paths \(\gamma(s)\) parameterized by arc length \(s \in [0, L]\) starting at any point on the boundary \(\Gamma\) and terminating at \(x\).

The characteristics (orthogonal trajectories of the level sets \(\{x \mid T(x) = c\}\)) satisfy:

\[\frac{d x(s)}{ds} = F(x) \frac{\nabla T(x)}{|\nabla T(x)|}\]

Because \(F(x) > 0\), the arrival time function \(T(x)\) is strictly non-decreasing along trajectories, precluding characteristics from turning backward.

docs.title: 3. Discretization and Numerical Schemes
docs.text: Direct central differences applied to \(|\nabla T| = 1/F\) produce numerical instabilities and fail to satisfy entropy conditions at shock formations (where wave fronts collide). A correct viscosity solution must employ an upwind finite difference scheme that respects the domain of dependence.

docs.title: 3.1 Upwind Finite Difference Operator in \(\mathbb{R}^2\)
docs.text:
Consider a regular Cartesian grid with spacing \(\Delta x\) and \(\Delta y\). Let \(T_{i,j} \approx T(i\Delta x, j\Delta y)\).

The Rouy-Tourin / Sethian first-order upwind discretization of \(|\nabla T|^2 = \frac{1}{F^2}\) is formulated as:

\[\left[ \max\left( D_{ij}^{-x} T, -D_{ij}^{+x} T, 0 \right) \right]^2 + \left[ \max\left( D_{ij}^{-y} T, -D_{ij}^{+y} T, 0 \right) \right]^2 = \frac{1}{F_{ij}^2}\]

where the standard forward and backward difference operators are defined as:

\[D_{ij}^{-x} T = \frac{T_{i,j} - T_{i-1,j}}{\Delta x}, \quad D_{ij}^{+x} T = \frac{T_{i+1,j} - T_{i,j}}{\Delta x}\] \[D_{ij}^{-y} T = \frac{T_{i,j} - T_{i,j-1}}{\Delta y}, \quad D_{ij}^{+y} T = \frac{T_{i,j+1} - T_{i,j}}{\Delta y}\]

docs.title: 3.2 Quadratic Formulation for Grid Updates
docs.text:
For isotropic cells (\(\Delta x = \Delta y = h\)), define the minimum upstream values along each axis:

\[T_x = \min(T_{i-1,j}, T_{i+1,j})\] \[T_y = \min(T_{i,j-1}, T_{i,j+1})\]

Assume without loss of generality that \(T_x \le T_y\). The update equation simplifies to the algebraic quadratic form:

\[(T - T_x)^2 + (T - T_y)^2 = \frac{h^2}{F_{ij}^2}\]

Expanding gives:

\[2T^2 - 2(T_x + T_y)T + (T_x^2 + T_y^2) - \frac{h^2}{F_{ij}^2} = 0\]

Solving for \(T\) via the quadratic formula yields:

\[T = \frac{T_x + T_y + \sqrt{(T_x + T_y)^2 - 2\left( T_x^2 + T_y^2 - \frac{h^2}{F_{ij}^2} \right)}}{2} = \frac{T_x + T_y + \sqrt{2\frac{h^2}{F_{ij}^2} - (T_x - T_y)^2}}{2}\]

docs.title: Validity Condition (Dimensional Degeneracy Check)
docs.text:
The two-dimensional characteristic wave reaches \((i,j)\) simultaneously from both axes if and only if the discriminant is strictly non-negative and \(T > T_y\):

\[|T_x - T_y| < \frac{h}{F_{ij}}\]

If this condition fails (\(T_y - T_x \ge \frac{h}{F_{ij}}\)), information propagates strictly along the 1D direction from \(T_x\), collapsing the update to:

\[T = T_x + \frac{h}{F_{ij}}\]

docs.title: 4. Algorithmic Architecture
docs.text:
The Fast Marching Method mimics Dijkstra's shortest-path algorithm over a continuous grid. The mesh nodes \(\mathcal{N}\) are partitioned into three mutually exclusive sets:

  1. \(\mathcal{K}\) (Known / Frozen): Nodes where the exact arrival time \(T\) has been computed and fixed.
  2. \(\mathcal{T}\) (Trial / Narrow Band): Immediate neighbors of \(\mathcal{K}\) whose provisional values have been computed; tracked inside a min-priority heap.
  3. \(\mathcal{F}\) (Far / Unvisited): Nodes that have not yet been evaluated (\(T = \infty\)).
[  F A R  ]  --->  [ T R I A L (Heap) ]  --->  [ K N O W N ]
T = Infinity        Monitored Candidates        Frozen Values

docs.title: 4.1 Algorithmic Procedure
docs.text:
Algorithm: Multi-Label Fast Marching with Obstacle Constraints
-------------------------------------------------------------------------
Input:  - Domain Grid of size N x M with spacing h
        - Seed Footprints: S_k for each building k in {1, ..., K}
        - Propagation Speeds: F_k (derived from TFA)
        - Boundary Blocks / Parcel Mask: B_mask
Output: - Arrival Time Field T(x, y)
        - Label Allocation Field L(x, y)

1. Initialization:
   For every grid node (i, j):
       If (i, j) in S_k (inside footprint of building k):
           T[i, j] = 0.0
           L[i, j] = k
           State[i, j] = KNOWN
       Else if (i, j) outside parcel boundary B_mask:
           T[i, j] = Infinity
           L[i, j] = -1
           State[i, j] = OBSTACLE
       Else:
           T[i, j] = Infinity
           L[i, j] = 0
           State[i, j] = FAR

2. Populate Narrow Band (Trial):
   Initialize Min-Priority Heap Q
   For each node (i, j) in KNOWN:
       For each orthogonal neighbor (ni, nj) in 4-neighborhood of (i, j):
           If State[ni, nj] == FAR:
               Compute T_trial using Quadratic Update with F = F[L[i, j]]
               T[ni, nj] = T_trial
               L[ni, nj] = L[i, j]
               State[ni, nj] = TRIAL
               Insert (ni, nj, T_trial) into Q

3. Marching Loop:
   While Q is not empty:
       Pop (ci, cj) with minimal T from Q
       State[ci, cj] = KNOWN

       For each orthogonal neighbor (ni, nj) of (ci, cj):
           If State[ni, nj] == OBSTACLE or State[ni, nj] == KNOWN:
               Continue

           parent_label = L[ci, cj]
           local_speed  = F[parent_label]
           T_candidate  = SolveQuadraticEikonal(ni, nj, local_speed)

           If State[ni, nj] == FAR:
               T[ni, nj] = T_candidate
               L[ni, nj] = parent_label
               State[ni, nj] = TRIAL
               Insert (ni, nj, T_candidate) into Q
           Else if State[ni, nj] == TRIAL:
               If T_candidate < T[ni, nj]:
                   T[ni, nj] = T_candidate
                   L[ni, nj] = parent_label
                   DecreaseKey((ni, nj), T_candidate) in Q

4. Return Fields T and L.

docs.title: 4.2 Computational Complexity
docs.text:
For a grid containing \(N\) total elements: - Each node enters and exits the TRIAL heap at most once. - Inserting and deleting minimum elements from a binary min-heap requires \(\mathcal{O}(\log |\mathcal{T}|)\) operations. - Since \(|\mathcal{T}| \le N\), total algorithmic time complexity is:

\[\mathcal{O}(N \log N)\]

Using advanced priority structures (e.g., untidy priority queues or Fibonacci heaps) can theoretically lower the amortized complexity toward \(\mathcal{O}(N)\), though standard binary heaps remain optimal in practical spatial memory layouts.

docs.title: 5. Overcoming Voronoi Pathologies in Urban Blocks
5.1 Prevention of Submerged Sites
docs.text:
In conventional Voronoi configurations, if building \(A\) has weight \(w_A \gg w_B\), the condition \(\|x - p_B\| - w_B > \|x - p_A\| - w_A\) can hold over the entirety of \(\Omega\), leaving site \(B\) with no cell (\(\emptyset\)).

In the FMM framework: - Footprint \(B\) is explicitly seeded at initialization: \(\forall x \in \text{Footprint}_B \implies T(x) = 0\). - By causality of the upwind scheme, \(T(x) \ge 0\) everywhere. - Consequently, site \(B\) retains its base footprint area:

\[\text{Area}(\text{Cell}_B) \ge \text{Area}(\text{Footprint}_B) > 0\]

docs.title: 5.2 Prevention of Site Eviction
docs.text:
Because every building centroid \(p_i\) is embedded within \(\text{Footprint}_i\), and that footprint is initialized with \(L(x) = i\), the point \(p_i\) is geometrically guaranteed to reside within its assigned allocation zone:

\[p_i \in \text{Footprint}_i \subseteq \text{Cell}_i\]

docs.title: 5.3 Immunity to Topological Leakage (Wrapping Effect)
docs.text:
Consider an irregular triangular block with three adjacent buildings along one edge: a large mall (\(M\)), a medium house (\(H_1\)), and a small house (\(H_2\)).

                      / \
                     /   \
                    /     \   <-- Open triangular interior
                   /       \
                  /  [H2]   \
                 /   [H1]    \
                /____[M]______\
  • In Euclidean Voronoi: The high weight of \(M\) projects radially outwards. The metric circle/hyperbola of \(M\) expands through the empty interior, wrapping around \(H_1\) and \(H_2\) to seize the vacant space directly behind \(H_2\).
  • In Obstacle-Constrained FMM:
  • The footprints of \(H_1\) and \(H_2\) are impenetrable barriers.
  • Any characteristic ray originating from \(M\) attempting to reach the space behind \(H_2\) must curve around the obstacle chain, satisfying the geodesic boundary condition:
\[L_{\text{geodesic}}(M \to \text{Behind } H_2) \gg L_{\text{geodesic}}(H_2 \to \text{Behind } H_2)\]
  1. Even if \(F_M \gg F_{H_2}\), the travel time \(T(x) = \int \frac{1}{F} ds\) for \(H_2\) over an infinitesimal distance directly adjacent to its back wall is near zero (\(T \approx \epsilon\)), whereas the mall's wave front must traverse the physical perimeter distance. \(H_2\) naturally captures its immediate contextual surroundings.

docs.title: 6. Implementation Notes: Parameterizing Speed from TFA
docs.text: To map Total Floor Area (TFA) to the continuous propagation speed \(F_k\), avoid simple linear mappings if weight disparities span multiple orders of magnitude.

docs.title: 6.1 Recommended Speed Scaling Formulations
docs.text:
Let \(\text{TFA}_k\) be the total floor area of building \(k\), and let \(A_{\text{fp}, k}\) be the base footprint ground area.

  1. Sub-linear / Square-Root Scaling (Recommended): Ground allocation grows in two dimensions (\(L \propto \sqrt{\text{Area}}\)). Map speed to equivalent linear expansion:
\[F_k = F_{\text{base}} \cdot \left( \frac{\text{TFA}_k}{\overline{\text{TFA}}} \right)^{1/2}\]
  1. Logarithmic Scaling (For Extreme Density Disparities): When high-rise towers (\(\text{TFA} \sim 100{,}000\text{ m}^2\)) neighbor single-story structures (\(\text{TFA} \sim 100\text{ m}^2\)):
\[F_k = F_{\text{base}} \cdot \left( 1 + \alpha \ln\left( 1 + \frac{\text{TFA}_k}{A_{\text{fp}, k}} \right) \right)\]

docs.title: 6.2 Target Area Termination Condition
docs.text: If each building has an upper bound quota \(A_k^{\max}\), augment step 3 of the Marching Loop: - Maintain an active counter of allocated cells \(C_k = \sum \mathbb{I}(L = k)\). - Once \(C_k \ge \frac{A_k^{\max}}{h^2}\), freeze expansion for label \(k\) by setting \(F_k \to 0\). - Remaining unallocated space is dynamically absorbed by neighboring active fronts.
